::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 .low}

explicit start marker <br/>
end indicated by `gap' between signals

:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3 .low}

type field indicates which next layer in use <br/>
often varies on frame-by-frame basis

:::


::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 .low}

actually `type/length` for historical reasons<br/>
but most commonly just used for type these days

:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5 .low}

*  destination address indicates who frame is for
*  present regardless of whether switching is in use
*  each host _filters_ out frames for "wrong" addresses

:::

::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6 .low}

since destination address always present<br/>
switches can always send every frame to everyone

(just less efficient)

:::


::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7 .low}

*  who the frame came from
*  gives "return address"

:::


::: {.myoverbox .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=8 .low}

*  sometimes extra stuff ("tags")
*  (used for VLANs, which is a topic for much later)

:::


### MAC addresses  {.smaller}


* MAC [media access control] addresses
* used by Ethernet, Wifi, and lots of other protocols
* 48-bit number written in hex: <code>01:23:45:67:89:AB</code> 

   * (sometimes seperated with <code>-</code> instead of <code>:</code>)

* assigned by IEEE to networking manufacturers in blocks 

   * Institution of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
   * example: <code>00:02:B3:</code>…, <code>00:03:47:</code>…, (and many more) for Intel
 
<hr class="vspace" />
* individual addresses hard-coded in networking hardware 

   * uniquely identify port/device



### special MAC addresses  {.smaller}


* <code>00:00:00:00:00:00</code> (all zeroes)
* <code>FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF</code> (all ones), <code>FF:</code>… 

   * special destination meaning ‘‘send to everyone’’ (on this network)
   * called <i>broadcast</i>

* <code>01:80:C2:</code>…, <code>33:33:</code>…, (and some more) 

   * special destinations representing multiple receivers
   * example: ‘all IPv6 routers on this network’ (<code>33:33:00:00:00:02</code>)
   * called <i>multicast</i>



### larger MAC addresses  {.smaller}


* IEEE now calls MAC address EUI-48 (48-bit Extended Unique Identifier) 
<hr class="vspace" />
* also created EUI-64, with 64-bit addresses 

   * way of mapping EUI-48s to EUI-64s
   * turns out 48 bits might have been low

* I'm not sure what status is on switching to 64-bit addresses 

   * IEEE 802.15.4 (used in ZigBee, 6LoWPAN, some others) uses EUI-64
   * I don't know other local network protocols that do
